blocks.text: A single graph can hold more information than a whole paragraph of description. Give a physicist a velocity-time graph of a BRT bus journey and, without any equations, they can read off the acceleration at every moment and the total distance from Ikorodu to CMS.

blocks.markdown:
Two graphs matter in this topic, and the trick is knowing which quantity the **gradient** and the **area** give you in each case.

On a **displacement-time** graph, gradient $= \frac{\Delta s}{\Delta t} = $ **velocity**. Area under it has no physical meaning.

On a **velocity-time** graph, gradient $= \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = $ **acceleration**, and the area between the line and the time axis $= $ **distance travelled**.

blocks.title: Gradient and area
blocks.text: Displacement-time: gradient = velocity. Velocity-time: gradient = acceleration, area = distance. Learn this pair as one sentence — nearly every graph question in WAEC and JAMB is answered by choosing the right one of the three.

rows: Body is at rest — displacement is not changing
Uniform velocity in the positive direction
Uniform velocity in the negative direction (returning)
Velocity increasing — the body is accelerating
Velocity decreasing — the body is decelerating

blocks.markdown:
### Finding distance from the area

Split the area into triangles, rectangles and trapezia.

- Triangle: $\frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$
- Rectangle: $\text{base} \times \text{height}$
- Trapezium: $\frac{1}{2}(a + b)h$, where $a$ and $b$ are the two parallel sides

For a journey that accelerates, cruises and then decelerates, the whole shape is one trapezium, so you can often do it in a single step.

blocks.caption: Trapezium rule applied to the area under a velocity-time graph

blocks.title: A three-stage journey
blocks.prompt: A bus starts from rest and accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s in 5.0 s. It then travels at 20 m/s for 10.0 s, and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in a further 5.0 s. Find (a) the acceleration in the first stage and (b) the total distance travelled.

steps.text: Sketch the velocity-time graph: it rises from the origin to 20 m/s at t = 5 s, stays flat until t = 15 s, then falls to zero at t = 20 s. The shape is a trapezium.
For (a), the acceleration is the gradient of the first section.
Evaluate the acceleration with its unit.
For (b), identify the parallel sides of the trapezium: the total time along the bottom is 20 s and the flat top runs from 5 s to 15 s, a length of 10 s. The height is the velocity, 20 m/s.
Evaluate, remembering that m/s × s gives metres.

blocks.markdown:
### Instantaneous values from a curve

When the graph is curved, the gradient changes from point to point. To find the velocity at one instant on a curved displacement-time graph, draw a **tangent** at that point and find the gradient of the tangent.

Use a long tangent line — a short one makes the two coordinates you read off close together, which magnifies your reading error.

blocks.title: WAEC and NECO tip
blocks.text: When a question says "from the graph, determine...", show your working on the graph itself: mark the triangle you used for the gradient and write the coordinates. Examiners award method marks for the construction even when the arithmetic slips.

points: On a displacement-time graph the gradient is the velocity; a horizontal line means the body is at rest.
On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled.
A downward slope on a velocity-time graph is retardation; a line below the time axis means motion in the opposite direction.
Find areas by splitting into triangles, rectangles and trapezia, using ½(a + b)h for a trapezium.
For a curved graph, find an instantaneous gradient by drawing a long tangent at the point of interest.
